2. Bringing legal protection of endangered species under Federal law.
3. Extending the Secretary's authority to control of the taking of endangered animals on the high seas by persons subject to the jurisdiction of the United States.
4. Generally tightens controls of the Federal Government over interstate and foreign commerce involving endangered species.
5. Restores the authority of the Secretary to acquire lands and waters with Land and Water Conservation Funds for protection, management, and development of habitat for endangered species.
6. Directs all Federal agencies to avoid wherever possible jeopardizing the continued existence of any endangered species by any projects in which that agency has an interest. This implies that the welfare of any endangered species should receive special consideration in the execution of Federal projects.
All of these provisions have economic implications either directly through benefits to endangered and other species that are of economic interest to man or through the value of resources which may be foregone or inhanced by the recovery of an endangered animal.
Following are areas of economic interest which illustrate the effect of the proposed legislation on the economy. As used earlier in illustrating the physical environment, areas of economic interest are developed from consideration of histories, existing conditions, and proposed future measures for protection and management of species and subspecies included in the 1973 edition of Threatened Wildlife of the United States.
